Recursive Reasoning Dataset Workflow

Install Blog GitHub

Recursive Reasoning Dataset Workflow

This tutorial shows the practical dataset path for structured recursive reasoning tasks.

Use it when you are building a benchmark adapter such as N-Queens, Graph Coloring, Sudoku, ARC-style grids, or another discrete reasoning task.

See also:

  • Recursive Reasoning Dataset API
  • Recursive Reasoning Docs
  • gollek-ml-recursive-reasoning API Reference

Step 1: Emit Generic Token Examples

Start by converting benchmark-specific examples into DiscreteTokenDatasetExample.

List<DiscreteTokenDatasetExample> examples = List.of(
    new DiscreteTokenDatasetExample(
        "graph-coloring",
        0,
        new int[] {0, -1, -1, 1},
        new int[] {0, 2, 1, 1},
        3,
        Map.of("nodeCount", 4, "colorCount", 3)
    ),
    new DiscreteTokenDatasetExample(
        "nqueens",
        1,
        new int[] {-1, 2, -1, -1},
        new int[] {1, 2, 0, 3},
        1,
        Map.of("size", 4)
    )
);

The generic example record is the handoff point between benchmark adapters and trainer utilities.

Step 2: Profile Before Splitting

Profile the full dataset before deciding on batch size or split policy.

DiscreteTokenDatasetProfile profile =
    DiscreteTokenDatasetProfiler.profile(examples);

System.out.println("examples=" + profile.exampleCount());
System.out.println("tasks=" + profile.taskExampleCounts());
System.out.println("max input length=" + profile.inputLengths().maxLength());
System.out.println("known-solution coverage=" + profile.knownSolutionCoverageRate());

Use the profile to check:

  • whether task distribution looks balanced
  • whether token ranges match the benchmark codec
  • whether known solution counts are available for coverage metrics
  • whether length-sorted batching is likely to reduce padding

Step 3: Split Deterministically

For the standard path, let the planner build the split and epochs together:

DiscreteTokenDatasetPlanConfig config =
    DiscreteTokenDatasetPlanConfig.stratifiedLengthSorted(
        0.10,
        0.10,
        2026L,
        32,
        64,
        -1
    );

DiscreteTokenDatasetPlan plan =
    DiscreteTokenDatasetPlanner.plan(examples, config);

DiscreteTokenDatasetPlanDiagnostics diagnostics = plan.diagnostics();
System.out.println("status=" + diagnostics.status());
System.out.println("ready=" + diagnostics.isReadyForTraining());
System.out.println("warnings=" + diagnostics.warnings());
System.out.println("task splits=" + diagnostics.taskSplits());
Map<String, Object> datasetMetadata = diagnostics.toMetadata();

DiscreteTokenDatasetPlanDiagnosticsPolicy ciPolicy =
    DiscreteTokenDatasetPlanDiagnosticsPolicy.defaults()
        .withHighPaddingRateThreshold(0.25);
DiscreteTokenDatasetPlanDiagnostics ciDiagnostics =
    plan.diagnostics(ciPolicy);

DiscreteTokenDatasetPlanReadinessReport readiness =
    plan.readiness(DiscreteTokenDatasetPlanReadinessGate.strict());
readiness.requireAccepted();

DiscreteTokenDatasetFingerprint fingerprint = plan.fingerprint();
System.out.println("dataset plan=" + fingerprint.shortValue());

Map<String, Object> checkpointFingerprintMetadata = fingerprint.toMetadata();
DiscreteTokenDatasetFingerprint expectedFingerprint =
    DiscreteTokenDatasetFingerprint.fromMetadata(checkpointFingerprintMetadata);
DiscreteTokenDatasetFingerprintMatch resumeMatch =
    plan.verifyFingerprint(expectedFingerprint);
resumeMatch.requireMatch();

DiscreteTokenDatasetPlanReport report =
    plan.report(DiscreteTokenDatasetPlanReadinessGate.strict());
Map<String, Object> preflightMetadata = report.toMetadata();
report.verifyFingerprintMetadataSection(preflightMetadata).requireMatch();

Path checkpointDir = Path.of("checkpoints/run-001");
DiscreteTokenDatasetTrainerProvenanceSpec provenance =
    DiscreteTokenDatasetTrainerProvenanceSpec.builder(checkpointDir, plan)
        .strict()
        .experimentName("gram-structured-reasoning")
        .runId("run-001")
        .seed(2026L)
        .checkpointStep(12L)
        .exactResumeExpectation()
        .build();
DiscreteTokenDatasetCheckpointManifest manifest = provenance.manifest();
Map<String, Object> checkpointMetadata = manifest.toMetadata();
provenance.writeManifest();
Map<String, Object> loadedCheckpointMetadata = provenance.readManifestMetadata();
DiscreteTokenDatasetCheckpointManifestSnapshot snapshot =
    provenance.readSnapshot();
snapshot.requireCurrentSchema();
snapshot.verifyPlan(plan).requireMatch();
snapshot.requireDatasetAccepted();
DiscreteTokenDatasetCheckpointResumeReport resumeReport =
    snapshot.resumeReport(plan);
resumeReport.requireReady();
DiscreteTokenDatasetCheckpointResumeExpectation expectedCheckpoint =
    provenance.resumeExpectation();
snapshot.resumeReport(plan, expectedCheckpoint).requireReady();
DiscreteTokenDatasetPlanReport currentStrictReport =
    plan.report(DiscreteTokenDatasetPlanReadinessGate.strict());
snapshot.resumeReport(currentStrictReport, expectedCheckpoint).requireReady();
DiscreteTokenDatasetCheckpointResumePolicy resumePolicy =
    provenance.resumePolicy();
DiscreteTokenDatasetCheckpointResumeReport policyReport =
    provenance.requireResumeReadyAndWriteReport();
DiscreteTokenDatasetCheckpointResumeReportSnapshot persistedResumeAudit =
    provenance.readResumeReportSnapshot();
persistedResumeAudit.requireReady();
DiscreteTokenDatasetTrainerCheckpointSnapshot checkpointAudit =
    provenance.readCheckpointSnapshot();
checkpointAudit.requireReady();
DiscreteTokenDatasetTrainerCheckpointInventory checkpointInventory =
    DiscreteTokenDatasetTrainerCheckpointInventory.scan(checkpointDir.getParent());
DiscreteTokenDatasetTrainerCheckpointSnapshot latestReadyCheckpoint =
    checkpointInventory.requireLatestReadyCheckpoint();
DiscreteTokenDatasetTrainerCheckpointSelectionPolicy checkpointSelection =
    DiscreteTokenDatasetTrainerCheckpointSelectionPolicy.latestResumeReady()
        .withExpectation(provenance.resumeExpectation());
DiscreteTokenDatasetTrainerCheckpointSnapshot latestResumeReadyCheckpoint =
    checkpointSelection.require(checkpointInventory);
DiscreteTokenDatasetTrainerCheckpointInspectionReport checkpointInspection =
    DiscreteTokenDatasetTrainerCheckpointInspectionReport.inspect(
        checkpointInventory,
        checkpointSelection);
checkpointInspection.requireSelectedCheckpoint();
Map<String, Object> resumeAuditMetadata = policyReport.toMetadata();
Map<String, Object> trainerMetadata =
    provenance.attachToTrainingMetadata(Map.of("runId", "run-001"), policyReport);
DiscreteTokenDatasetTrainerProvenanceListener provenanceListener =
    provenance.listener();
// Pass provenanceListener to a canonical trainer via .listener(provenanceListener).
TrainingSummary enrichedSummary =
    provenanceListener.lastEnrichedSummary().orElse(null);
Map<String, Object> resumePolicyMetadata = resumePolicy.toMetadata();
DiscreteTokenDatasetCheckpointResumePolicy reloadedResumePolicy =
    DiscreteTokenDatasetCheckpointResumePolicy.fromMetadata(resumePolicyMetadata);
reloadedResumePolicy.requireReady(loadedCheckpointMetadata, plan);
String resumeAuditJson =
    DiscreteTokenDatasetCheckpointMetadataJson.toPrettyJson(resumeAuditMetadata);

For a mixed benchmark dataset, prefer a task-stratified split.

DiscreteTokenDatasetSplit split =
    DiscreteTokenDatasetSplitter.stratifiedShuffledByFractions(
        examples,
        0.10,
        0.10,
        2026L
    );

For a single-task dataset, a regular shuffled split is enough:

DiscreteTokenDatasetSplit split =
    DiscreteTokenDatasetSplitter.shuffledByFractions(
        examples,
        0.10,
        0.10,
        2026L
    );

Check each partition:

System.out.println(plan.split().trainProfile().taskExampleCounts());
System.out.println(plan.split().validationProfile().taskExampleCounts());
System.out.println(plan.split().testProfile().taskExampleCounts());

Step 4: Build Trainer Epochs

The planner already built the recommended epochs:

DiscreteTokenDatasetEpoch trainEpoch = plan.trainEpoch();
DiscreteTokenDatasetEpoch validationEpoch = plan.validationEpoch();
DiscreteTokenDatasetEpoch testEpoch = plan.testEpoch();

If you are not using the planner, build epochs directly:

DiscreteTokenDatasetEpoch trainEpoch =
    DiscreteTokenDatasetEpochBatcher.lengthSorted(
        split.trainExamples(),
        32,
        -1,
        false
    );

Track padding efficiency:

System.out.println("train padding rate=" + plan.diagnostics().trainPaddingRate());
System.out.println("train padding tokens=" + plan.diagnostics().trainPaddingTokenCount());

Use diagnostics before a long run to catch empty validation/test splits, dropped training examples from dropLast, missing known-solution counts, or a training padding rate that is higher than expected. For mixed-task datasets, inspect taskSplits() to confirm each task is represented in the expected partitions. Use DiscreteTokenDatasetPlanDiagnosticsPolicy.lenient() for exploratory datasets where validation/test or known-solution coverage is intentionally absent, and a stricter custom threshold for CI or production trainers. Use DiscreteTokenDatasetPlanReadinessGate.training() when warnings should be reported but not fail a run, or strict() when warnings should block CI. Persist plan.fingerprint().toMetadata() with checkpoints so resumed runs can verify the same config, split, examples, and epoch layout were used. Use DiscreteTokenDatasetFingerprint.fromMetadata(...) to recreate the stored fingerprint, then call plan.verifyFingerprint(expected).requireMatch() or plan.verifyFingerprintMetadata(metadata).requireMatch() before resuming. When the checkpoint stores the full plan.report(gate).toMetadata() payload, use verifyFingerprintMetadataSection(reportMetadata) to read the nested fingerprint section directly. Use plan.report(gate) when checkpoint metadata should include the fingerprint, diagnostics, and readiness decision together. Use DiscreteTokenDatasetCheckpointManifest.builder(report) when the checkpoint also needs experiment identity, run id, seed, step, and custom attributes. Use DiscreteTokenDatasetCheckpointManifestSnapshot.fromMetadata(metadata) when resume code needs to verify a persisted checkpoint manifest before loading weights or trainer state. Use snapshot.resumeReport(plan).requireReady() when the resume path should perform schema, dataset readiness, and fingerprint checks as one preflight gate. Use DiscreteTokenDatasetCheckpointResumeExpectation.builder() when resume code should also pin experiment identity, run id, model family, seed, or minimum checkpoint step. Pass snapshot.resumeReport(currentReport, expectation) when the current run should also fail if its freshly materialized report is blocked by a stricter readiness gate. Use DiscreteTokenDatasetCheckpointResumePolicy.strict().withExpectation(...) when trainer resume code wants one reusable gate that creates the current preflight report, checks identity, and fails fast before checkpoint state loads. Policy-evaluated resume reports include policyTracked() and policyMetadata() so audit payloads can record the gate and expectations that made the decision. Use resumePolicy.toMetadata() and DiscreteTokenDatasetCheckpointResumePolicy.fromMetadata(...) when resume policy settings come from trainer config, CI payloads, or checkpoint metadata. Use DiscreteTokenDatasetCheckpointMetadataJson.write(...), read(...), and readSnapshot(...) when those metadata maps should be persisted as stable JSON checkpoint artifacts without adding a JSON runtime dependency. Use DiscreteTokenDatasetCheckpointResumeReportSnapshot.fromMetadata(...) or DiscreteTokenDatasetTrainerCheckpointBridge.readResumeReportSnapshot(...) when CI, dashboards, or extensions need to inspect the persisted resume audit later without rebuilding the dataset plan. Use DiscreteTokenDatasetTrainerCheckpointBridge.readCheckpointSnapshot(...) when those tools should inspect the manifest and optional resume report sidecars together and distinguish manifest-only, ready, and blocked checkpoint states. Use DiscreteTokenDatasetTrainerCheckpointInventory.scan(rootDir) when CI or a dashboard should scan a parent directory of checkpoint runs and keep corrupt sidecars as read failures while still reporting the healthy runs. Use DiscreteTokenDatasetTrainerCheckpointSelectionPolicy.latestReady() when manifest-only checkpoints are acceptable, or latestResumeReady() when a restore must have an already persisted ready resume audit. Add withExpectation(...) to require the selected run, model family, seed, or checkpoint step. Use DiscreteTokenDatasetTrainerCheckpointInspectionReport.inspect(...) when a JBang inspector, CI job, or dashboard should show the selected restore target alongside accepted and rejected checkpoint candidates. Use DiscreteTokenDatasetTrainerCheckpointRestorePlan or the inspector restore section when resume code needs a compact handoff payload with the checkpoint paths, run identity, selection policy, and resume-report status. Use DiscreteTokenDatasetTrainerCheckpointRestorePreflight when resume code needs the final current-plan decision before opening checkpoint state. This catches cases where the selected checkpoint identity is acceptable but the fresh dataset fingerprint or readiness gate no longer matches. For terminal/CI flows, use the checkpoint inspector preflight section with currentReport=...; the report file can be a direct dataset plan report, checkpoint manifest, provenance metadata payload, or prior restore preflight JSON. Use the sibling explain currentReport=... section when the workflow needs a short, categorized decision payload with a primary finding code and suggested next steps. Use lineageChain for the selected checkpoint’s resolved root-to-leaf ancestry and lineageGraph when CI should fail or warn on duplicate run ids, missing parents, ambiguous parent references, parent identity mismatches, or cycles across the checkpoint root. Use lineageHealth when CI needs the same health gate without the full node list; read issueDetails for the affected checkpoint paths, stable issue codes, severity, blocking status, actions, and mismatch reasons. Use the top-level kind and schemaVersion fields to pin the health payload contract in CI or dashboard parsers. Java consumers can rehydrate the same payload with DiscreteTokenDatasetCheckpointLineageHealthSnapshot instead of parsing raw maps, or publish the bundled JSON Schema from jsonSchemaMetadata() for external validators. Use the inspector’s lineageHealthValidation section, or DiscreteTokenDatasetCheckpointLineageHealthValidationReport from Java, when CI needs a compact valid/invalid payload rather than the full health payload. Use lineageHealthSchema or lineageHealthValidationSchema when the same workflow needs a single schema, lineageHealthSchemaCatalog for compact contract discovery, lineageHealthSchemas when it should discover both health contracts with embedded schemas, and lineageHealthSchemaCatalogSchema when the catalog shape itself should be pinned. The catalog includes a bundle-level schemaSetSha256, per-schema SHA-256 digests, and byte counts for drift checks. Use lineageHealthSchemaLock for the smallest stable lock payload and lineageHealthSchemaLockSchema when that lock shape should be pinned too. Use lineageHealthSchemaLockValidation schemaLock=/path/to/lock.json to compare a saved lock against the current schema bundle before automation consumes a lineage-health payload, add requireSchemaLockValid=true when drift should fail the command, and lineageHealthSchemaLockValidationSchema to pin the validator report shape. The validation report includes its schema id/resource and both lock-schema ids, which keeps archived CI logs self-describing. Use issueCodes, issueDetailCount, and blockingIssueCount for compact CI summaries, and primaryIssueCode with primaryIssueAction for the headline failure. Use healthScore, alertLevel, and healthBadge when a dashboard needs a compact lineage status pill. Use checks, failingChecks, and checkSummary when it needs category-level lineage invariant rows, primary failing-check identity, type, action, full check payload, or severity rollups; those priority-aware primary failing-check fields are also mirrored at the top level of lineageHealth. Add requireLineageHealthy=true in inspector commands, or withFailOnLineageIssues(true) in Java selection policies, when unhealthy lineage should block checkpoint selection. Use the checkpoint demo’s clean lineage-unhealthy mode when CI examples need a deterministic missing-parent fixture for lineageHealth failure payloads. Keep the default resumeMode=strict for normal training. Use resumeMode=compatible for warning-only current-plan gates, and resumeMode=force only when a research/debug run intentionally accepts compatibility warnings. Use DiscreteTokenDatasetTrainerProvenanceSpec.builder(checkpointDir, plan) for the normal trainer integration path: it creates the report, manifest, resume policy, checkpoint sidecar helpers, restore-plan selection helpers, and lifecycle listener from one reusable object. Use DiscreteTokenDatasetTrainerCheckpointBridge.writeManifest(...), requireResumeReadyAndWriteReport(...), and attachToTrainingMetadata(...) when recursive-reasoning dataset provenance should live beside the normal trainer checkpoint files and appear in trainer summary metadata. Use DiscreteTokenDatasetTrainerProvenanceListener.builder(...) when that same workflow should run from trainer lifecycle callbacks and fail fast before training overwrites an incompatible dataset manifest. Use toMetadata() when the trainer needs to persist the dataset-plan health next to checkpoints or reports.

Step 5: Convert One Batch To Backend Tensors

DiscreteTokenDatasetBatch is still Java-array based. Convert it at the last responsible moment.

DiscreteTokenDatasetBatch batch = trainEpoch.batches().get(0);

int[][] inputIds = batch.inputTokens();
int[][] targetIds = batch.targetTokens();
int[][] inputMask = batch.inputMask();
int[][] targetMask = batch.targetMask();

From here, a concrete trainer can convert arrays into the tensor backend it owns:

  • Gollek tensor/autograd tensors
  • ONNX input tensors
  • SafeTensor-backed model inputs
  • LiteRT or GGUF runner inputs
  • external research tensors

The dataset API does not pick that backend for you.

Step 6: Keep Evaluation Metadata

Known solution counts and metadata stay available through the batch:

for (int row = 0; row < batch.batchSize(); row++) {
    if (batch.hasKnownSolutionCount(row)) {
        int solutions = batch.knownSolutionCounts()[row];
        Map<String, Object> metadata = batch.metadata().get(row);
        // attach to trainer reports or coverage evaluation
    }
}

This is important for GRAM-style width-scaling experiments, where valid-rate and unique-solution coverage are usually as important as the scalar loss.

Recommended Policy

For first experiments:

Stage Recommendation
Dataset shape DiscreteTokenDatasetExample
Standard planner DiscreteTokenDatasetPlanner.plan(...)
Planner config DiscreteTokenDatasetPlanConfig.stratifiedLengthSorted(...)
Pre-training checks plan.diagnostics()
Manual diagnostics DiscreteTokenDatasetProfiler.profile(...)
Manual mixed task split stratifiedShuffledByFractions(..., seed)
Manual training epoch lengthSorted(..., batchSize, padToken, dropLast)
Tensor conversion trainer-owned adapter after batching

Next Step

After the dataset workflow works, wire the batches into a model-specific trainer adapter. Keep the benchmark codec, dataset planning, tensor conversion, and model forward pass as separate layers so future tasks can reuse the same dataset path.
